lessons.title: How the Internet Remembers
lessons.content_md:
# How the Internet Remembers 🧠

When you turn off your computer, it doesn't forget your files. When you close the Instagram app, your photos don't disappear.

This is because of **Storage**. Storage is how computers remember things permanently. In the Cloud, storage is incredibly important because there are billions of people generating mountains of data every single second.

But not all data is the same!

## Structured vs. Unstructured Data

Cloud engineers divide all data in the world into two main types:

### 1. Structured Data 📊
This is data that fits perfectly into a spreadsheet. It has rows and columns. 
- **Examples:** A list of users (Name, Email, Age), your bank account transactions (Date, Amount, Merchant), or a store's inventory.
- Structured data is highly organized and easy to search.

### 2. Unstructured Data 🎨
This is everything else! It's data that doesn't fit into neat rows and columns. It's messy, large, and comes in all shapes and sizes.
- **Examples:** A 4K video of your dog, an MP3 music file, a PDF document, or a JPEG photo.

<flipcard front="🤔 Is an MP3 music file Structured or Unstructured data?" back="Unstructured! You can't easily fit the audio of a song into a spreadsheet column. It requires a different type of storage."></flipcard>

Because these two types of data are so different, the Cloud has two completely different ways to store them: **Databases** (for structured) and **Object Storage** (for unstructured).

lessons.title: Object Storage: Digital Lockers
lessons.content_md:
# Object Storage: Digital Lockers 🗄️

Let's talk about how the Cloud stores **Unstructured Data** (photos, videos, backups). It uses something called **Object Storage**.

## The Digital Locker Metaphor

Imagine a massive warehouse filled with millions of identical metal lockers. 

When you want to store a file (like a profile picture), you put it inside a locker. You put a lock on it, and the system hands you a unique key with a number on it (like `#9472A`). 

- It doesn't matter what's inside the locker (a tiny text file or a massive 10GB video). 
- The system doesn't organize the lockers by alphabetical order or by category. 
- The *only* way to get your file back is to hand the system your exact unique key.

This is how Object Storage works! Every file is an "Object." It gets dumped into a massive flat space, and the system gives you a unique URL to find it later.

<flipcard front="🗄️ How do you retrieve a file from Object Storage?" back="You must have the exact, unique URL (the 'key') assigned to that specific file. You can't easily 'search' inside Object Storage like you can in a database."></flipcard>

## Infinite Space

The superpower of Object Storage is that it is virtually **infinite** and very cheap. 

If you build a new social media app and suddenly 10 million people upload photos on day one, you don't need to panic or buy new hard drives. The Cloud provider's Object Storage just keeps accepting the files and giving you URLs back. It scales automatically!

## Real-World Example: Amazon S3

The most famous Object Storage in the world is **Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service)**. When you watch a movie on Netflix, the actual video file you are streaming is stored in a massive digital locker on Amazon S3!

lessons.title: Relational Databases: The Filing Cabinet
lessons.content_md:
# Relational Databases: The Filing Cabinet 📁

Now, let's talk about how the Cloud stores **Structured Data** (users, scores, transactions). It uses **Relational Databases**.

## The Highly Organized Filing Cabinet

Imagine the most organized filing cabinet in the world. Inside, there are folders, and inside those folders are perfectly lined-up spreadsheets.

One spreadsheet is called `Users` and has columns for ID, Name, and Email. 
Another spreadsheet is called `Purchases` and has columns for Purchase ID, User ID, and Item Name.

The magic of a relational database is that the spreadsheets talk to each other (they have "relationships"). Because the `Purchases` sheet includes a User ID, you can instantly ask the database a highly complex question:

> *"Give me a list of all the Names of Users who purchased an item called 'Magic Sword' in the last 24 hours."*

The database can search through millions of rows and give you the exact answer in a fraction of a second.

<flipcard front="📁 What is the main superpower of a Relational Database?" back="Its ability to quickly search, filter, and connect structured data across multiple tables (spreadsheets) using complex queries!"></flipcard>

## SQL: The Language of Databases

To talk to this organized filing cabinet, you use a special programming language called **SQL (Structured Query Language)**. 

When a developer writes `SELECT Name FROM Users WHERE Age > 18`, they are using SQL to filter the spreadsheet!

## Real-World Example: Amazon RDS

In the cloud, you don't want to install and manage your own database server. You use a managed service like **Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service)**. Amazon sets up the filing cabinet, backs it up automatically, and makes sure it never crashes, leaving you free to just write your SQL queries!
